message.content:
In Texas, tenants have several statutory protections and responsibilities under the Texas Property Code (Title 2, Subtitle B). Below is an overview of key rights and obligations you should know: | Category | Tenant Rights | Tenant Responsibilities | |----------|---------------|-------------------------| | **Security Deposit** | • Landlord may charge up to one month’s rent for residential units; two months for furnished units.
• Must be returned within 30 days after lease ends, minus deductions for damages beyond normal wear & tear.
• Landlord must provide a written itemized statement if withholding any portion. | • Keep the unit clean and free from damage.
• Provide proper notice before moving out (usually 30 days). | | **Habitability** | • Landlord must maintain plumbing, heating, electrical, structural integrity, and pest control.
• Must keep the premises safe and sanitary. | • Report needed repairs promptly.
• Maintain cleanliness and avoid causing damage. | | **Rent Payment** | • Rent is due on the date specified in the lease; late fees are allowed but cannot exceed 10% of the monthly rent. | • Pay rent on time.
• Keep records of payments. | | **Entry by Landlord** | • Landlord must give at least 24‑hour written notice before entering, except in emergencies.
• Entry is prohibited during “reasonable hours” unless otherwise agreed. | • Respect landlord’s right to enter with proper notice. | | **Lease Terms** | • Lease agreements must be in writing for leases longer than one year.
• Certain clauses (e.g., “no pets” or “no smoking”) are enforceable only if they comply with local ordinances. | • Sign a lease that reflects your understanding.
• Understand that verbal agreements can be difficult to enforce. | | **Discrimination** | • Protected against discrimination based on race, color, religion, sex, national origin, disability, familial status, or source of income (including public assistance). | • Provide truthful information when applying. | | **Eviction Process** | • Landlord must follow the formal eviction process: serve a written notice (e.g., 3‑day notice for nonpayment), file a lawsuit, obtain a judgment, then sheriff’s execution.
• Eviction cannot be carried out without a court order. | • Respond to notices promptly.
• Attend court hearings if required. | | **Right to Quiet Enjoyment** | • You have the right to use the premises without interference from the landlord or other tenants. | • Avoid activities that disturb neighbors or violate lease terms. | | **Repair and Deduct / Right to Repair** | • If landlord fails to repair, you may (under certain circumstances) pay for repairs and deduct cost from rent, but this is limited and requires following strict procedures. | • Document all repair requests and responses. | | **Subletting / Assignment** | • Generally allowed if the lease permits it or if the landlord consents. | • Obtain written consent if required. | | **Notice to Vacate** | • Landlord must give at least 30 days’ written notice for month‑to‑month tenancy termination. | • Provide written notice if you intend to move out. | ### Practical Tips 1. **Read Your Lease Carefully** – Even if it’s a short‑term rental, the lease is legally binding. 2. **Keep Records** – Photographs, receipts, emails, and text messages documenting condition and communication help protect you. 3. **Know Local Ordinances** – Some cities (e.g., Austin, Dallas) have additional tenant protections such as rent control or mandatory lead‑paint disclosures. 4. **Use Written Communication** – Whenever possible, communicate via email or text so you have a record. 5. **Seek Legal Aid** – If you face eviction or disputes, consider contacting a local tenant advocacy group or legal aid organization. --- #### Quick Reference: How to File a Complaint If you believe your landlord has violated your rights: 1. **Document the Issue** – Photos, videos, written complaints. 2. **Contact the Landlord** – Send a written complaint. 3. **File a Complaint with the Texas Attorney General’s Office** – For issues like unlawful evictions or discrimination. 4. **Consider Small Claims Court** – For disputes involving less than $20,000. Feel free to ask if you’d like more detail on any specific area—such as how to handle a security deposit dispute or what steps to take if you’re facing eviction.
